title: SRE surface-map, shortcuts, and rollback recipes (draft)
body:
Purpose
This is an operator-focused runbook draft intended to reduce decision time during API degradations. It prioritizes: 1) surfacing the right signal quickly, 2) low-risk shortcuts that restore customer-visible behavior, and 3) explicit rollback recipes for common remediation actions (model fallback, gateway throttles, stream-to-bulk conversion).

Scope
- Covers transient timeouts, client 429s from rate limits, degraded streaming (long gaps or truncated events), and elevated 5xx/error rates.
- Intended for SREs and on-call runtime engineers.
- Not a replacement for full postmortem; use for first-response and safe rollbacks.

Quick mental model (one-liner)
- Timeouts: often infra (network, overloaded GPU host, long KV cache miss) or kernel-level queuing.
- 429s: either client storm or internal rate-limiter/circuit-breaker firing; check upstream vs gateway.
- Degraded streaming: partial model progress or transport congestion; can be transient buffer exhaustion.
- Elevated 5xx: model crash, OOM, or bad inputs exposing edge-case failure.

Immediate triage checklist (first 10 minutes)
1) Announce on Slack: #sre-oncall, short subject, brief symptom, impact estimate. Example: "INC/alert: hosted-api 5xx spike (100 rps -> 5xx 20%) 02:14 UTC — estimating 15% of customers affected".
2) Capture impact: check Route/Model mapping in Console (which routes are seeing errors).
3) Verify synthetic canaries: are the synthetic probes failing? (Kibana: probes.index.success_rate < 90%).
4) Identify whether the errors originate at: edge (gateway/nginx), runtime (inference pod), or model (process crash).

Surface commands and quick signals
- API Gateway (fast check): curl -I https://api.redwood.inference/v1/health (look for 503 or 429 headers)
- Edge logs (last 5m): gcloud logging read "resource.type=internal_http_lb AND severity>=ERROR" --limit 200
- Runtime pods (kubectl): kubectl -n runtime get pods -o wide --selector=app=runtime | grep -E "CrashLoopBackOff|OOMKilled"
- Recent 5xx sample (ELB): aws elbv2 describe-target-health --target-group-arn <arn> --query 'TargetHealthDescriptions[?TargetHealth.State==\`unhealthy\`]'


Fast heuristics to answer "is it model or infra?"
- If only one model/variant shows 5xx while others unaffected -> likely model or model-specific config (quantization, kernel mismatch).
- If all models behind the same nodepool/instance type show elevated latency -> infra (GPU host pressure, kernel throttles).
- If 429s coincide with sudden spike in requests from a small set of API keys -> client-driven; consider temporary key throttles.

Immediate mitigation shortcuts (low-risk, reversible)
A) Circuit-break to slower but safer path (preferred first action)
- Flip route to a lower-capacity but more robust variant: Console -> Routes -> Route X -> Fallback -> enable "stable-variant-1". This avoids global rollback and preserves partial service.
- If Console unavailable, flip at the API Gateway: add request header mapping to route to direct to fallback (requires runbook ACL).

B) Temporarily increase gateway concurrency/leaky-bucket window (only if infra healthy)
- Adjust API gateway rate-limit config to allow short burst for affected routes. Watch CPU and socket counts.

C) Convert streaming to non-streaming (quickest way to restore client experience)
- For routes with progressive streaming failures, switch to chunked response fallback where runtime waits for final response and returns in one shot. In Console: Route -> Advanced -> streaming-mode: chunked.
- Pros: reduces per-connection pressure; cons: increases tail latency for long responses.

D) Scoped request shedding for abusive keys
- Identify keys with high qps: Kibana query: "client_api_key.keyword: \"abc123\" AND @timestamp:[now-15m TO now]"
- Add temporary ACL to reject that key or reduce quota.

Deeper troubleshooting (metrics and queries)
- Prometheus queries (examples):
  - 5xx rate by model: sum(rate(http_requests_total{status=~\"5..\",route=~\"/v1/.*\"}[5m])) by (model)
  - Latency p95 by route: histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m])) by (le, route))
  - Inference queue length: runtime_inflight_requests{pool=~\".*gpu.*\"}

- Kibana sample queries:
  - Errors last 15m: severity:ERROR AND service:runtime AND @timestamp:[now-15m TO now]
  - Streaming gaps: message:\"frame-drop\" OR message:\"stream-disconnect\"

- System checks on runtime node:
  - GPU utilization: nvidia-smi --query-gpu=utilization.gpu,utilization.memory --format=csv
  - Kernel saturation: sar -q 1 5 (load average/ctx switches)

Common remediation recipes (explicit rollback included)
1) Model variant fallback (safe, common)
- When to use: single-variant 5xx or regression after rollout.
- Steps: Console -> Routes -> select route -> set primary to previous stable variant -> save -> monitor metrics for 5m.
- Rollback: to undo, revert primary to new variant and schedule controlled canary once root cause fixed. Document rollout ID and PR that triggered change.

2) Runtime pod restart (targeted)
- When to use: pod shows OOM/CrashLoopBackOff or CPU stuck.
- Steps: kubectl -n runtime delete pod <pod-name> (or scale down deployment by 1 and back up).
- Rollback: if restart doesn't help, scale to zero then back to desired replica count to force fresh placement. Note in incident timeline which nodes were reused.

3) Gateway rate-limit adjustment (scoped)
- When to use: 429 flood caused by gateway limits but infra still healthy.
- Steps: increase limit for affected route by 2x with a 5-minute TTL; monitor error rate and socket saturation.
- Rollback: set value back to previous within Console or via infra-as-code commit (record changelist). If repeated, create follow-up to harden limits.

4) Streaming -> chunked switch (fast patch)
- When to use: streaming stalls, partial frames, client-facing truncations.
- Steps: flip route streaming-mode to chunked. Notify clients via status page if longer tail latencies expected.
- Rollback: switch mode back when streaming stable for >30m under load test.

Escalation matrix (who to call in order)
1) Oncall SRE (primary): see PagerDuty roster (use PD to call).
2) Runtime eng lead: Diego Martinez (slack: @diego) — model/kernel/quantization questions.
3) Serving runtime owner: Priya Nair (slack: @priya) — infra/placement/queueing.
4) Product owner (if behavior change needed): notify via #platform-product.

Operator keyboard shortcuts and handoff snippet
- Quick incident note to paste into postmortem: "Observed spike in route X: 5xx rate rose from 0.3% -> 12% between T0 and T0+7m. Temporary mitigation: switched route X to stable-variant-20260122; error rate dropped to 0.6% within 3m. Root cause hypothesis: kernel change in variant 20260201 triggered quantization edge case. Follow-ups: pin rollout, reproduce in staging, add unit test for large-batch kv-miss"

Communication best-practices during incident
- Keep updates short, timestamped, and include what changed and what you're planning next. Example: "03:12 UTC — applied fallback variant; monitoring p95 and 5xx; next: probe model logs for OOMs."
- Always post mitigation and owner for follow-up tasks.

Post-incident checklist (to run after service restored)
- Collect a 5-minute window of request payloads (sample) for failed vs successful requests.
- Trigger CI rollout of the implicated variant in canary with load-generators and capture KV/cache behavior.
- Create GH issue linking PR that deployed the variant and assign to runtime/model owner.
- Write short blameless postmortem stub in Confluence within 24h.

Open questions / TODOs in this draft
- Automate detection of model-specific 5xx signatures to suggest variant fallback automatically. (RDW-1256)
- Add an operator Console quick-action to toggle streaming mode without requiring route save confirm.
- Define safe default TTLs for gateway burst increases.

Notes to self
- Keep this doc minimal and focus on reversible actions. Long-term fixes belong in separate RFCs.
- If you used a 'hot patch' (gateway change or variant flip) capture exact diff and PR the change where possible so runs can be audited.

Appendix: useful snippets (copy/paste)
- curl health: curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code} %{time_total}\n' https://api.redwood.inference/v1/health
- check pod logs (last 200 lines): kubectl -n runtime logs <pod> --tail=200
- sample prometheus for errors by route: curl -g 'http://prometheus/api/v1/query?query=sum(rate(http_requests_total{status=~"5..",job="runtime"}[5m])) by (route)'
